| Serverless | Lambda | Functions | Cloud Functions |
| Containers | EKS | AKS | GKE |

GCP strengths: BigQuery (analytics), GKE (managed Kubernetes), TensorFlow/Vertex AI (ML), and global network. Pricing model uses sustained-use discounts automatically.
How do I connect to a wireless network that isn't showing up?

If a Wi-Fi network exists but doesn't appear in the list, it might be hidden or your adapter isn't detecting it.

**Connect to a hidden network:**
1. Settings > Network & Internet > Wi-Fi > 'Manage known networks' > 'Add network'.
2. Enter the exact network name (SSID), security type (usually WPA2-Personal or WPA3), and password.
3. Check 'Connect automatically' and click Save.

**If the network isn't hidden but still not showing:**
1. Toggle Wi-Fi off and on: Quick settings (Win+A) > turn Wi-Fi off, wait 10 seconds, turn it back on.

2. Check the Wi-Fi adapter: Device Manager > Network adapters. If your Wi-Fi adapter has a yellow warning icon, right-click > Update driver.

3. Check the frequency band: The network might be 5 GHz only, and your adapter only supports 2.4 GHz. Check your adapter's specs in Device Manager > Properties > Advanced > look for '802.11ac' or '802.11ax' (these support 5 GHz).

4. Reset the adapter: Disable and re-enable it in Device Manager.

5. Restart the router: Unplug it for 30 seconds and plug it back in.

6. Check if airplane mode is on: Quick settings > make sure airplane mode is off.

7. Run the network troubleshooter: Settings > System > Troubleshoot > Other troubleshooters > Network adapter.
How do I enable Hyper-V on Windows?

Hyper-V lets you run virtual machines natively:

**Requirements**: Windows 10/11 Pro, Enterprise, or Education (not Home). 64-bit CPU with SLAT support. At least 4 GB RAM.

**Enable it**:
1. Settings → Apps → Optional features → More Windows features → check 'Hyper-V' → OK → Restart.
2. Or via PowerShell (admin): `Enable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName Microsoft-Hyper-V -All`
3. Or via DISM: `DISM /Online /Enable-Feature /All /FeatureName:Microsoft-Hyper-V`

**After restart**:
- Open Hyper-V Manager from Start.
- Click 'Quick Create' for an easy VM setup, or 'New' → 'Virtual Machine' for full customization.
- Use Generation 2 VMs for UEFI support and better performance.

**Note**: Enabling Hyper-V may affect other virtualization software (VirtualBox, VMware). VirtualBox 6.1+ and VMware Workstation 15.5+ support running alongside Hyper-V.

**On Windows Home**: You can use this community script to enable Hyper-V, but it's unsupported by Microsoft.
A user accidentally deleted a file and it's not in the Recycle Bin. What recovery options exist?

Several options depending on the situation: 1) Check if File History is enabled—go to Control Panel → File History → Restore personal files, and browse to the folder to recover previous versions. 2) Right-click the parent folder → Properties → Previous Versions tab—Windows may have Volume Shadow Copies if System Restore is enabled. 3) If the file was in a OneDrive-synced folder, check OneDrive's web interface → Recycle Bin, which retains deleted files for 30 days (93 days for work accounts). 4) If none of the above work, use data recovery software like Recuva or TestDisk immediately—the longer you wait, the more likely the disk sectors get overwritten. 5) Stop using the drive to avoid overwriting the deleted data. 6) For critical business data, professional data recovery services can recover from even formatted drives, though this is expensive ($300–$1500+). Prevention: enable File History, use cloud sync, and implement regular backups.
How do I troubleshoot Group Policy not applying to a Windows workstation?

Step-by-step: 1) Verify domain connectivity: 'nltest /sc_query:domain.com'—should show 'Trusted DC Connection Status = 0 0x0 NERR_Success'. 2) Force a GP update: 'gpupdate /force'. 3) Generate a report: 'gpresult /H C:\gpresult.html' and open it in a browser. This shows: Applied GPOs (confirm your GPO is listed). Denied GPOs (with reasons—commonly security filtering). 4) Check common issues: Security filtering—the computer or user must be in a group that has 'Read' and 'Apply group policy' permissions on the GPO. WMI filter—if the GPO has a WMI filter, test it: 'wmic path Win32_OperatingSystem get Caption'. Link enabled—verify the GPO link is enabled in GPMC. GPO status—check it's not set to 'All settings disabled'. OU placement—verify the computer/user object is in the correct OU. 5) Check replication: 'repadmin /replsummary'—GPO changes must replicate to the DC the workstation is using. 6) Check Sysvol replication: the GPO files in \\domain\SYSVOL must be consistent across DCs. 7) Use Group Policy Modeling (in GPMC) to simulate what would apply. 8) Check event logs: Event Viewer → Applications and Services Logs → Microsoft → Windows → GroupPolicy → Operational.
How do I set up a distribution group vs a shared mailbox vs a Microsoft 365 group?

Each serves a different purpose: 1) **Distribution Group** — used for sending email to a group of people. No shared inbox or calendar. Good for announcements (e.g., all-company@). Create in Exchange admin center → Recipients → Groups. 2) **Shared Mailbox** — a dedicated mailbox that multiple users can access. Has its own email address, calendar, and sent items. No license required (up to 50GB). Great for team inboxes like support@ or info@. Create in Microsoft 365 admin center → Teams & groups → Shared mailboxes. Grant Full Access and Send As permissions to the relevant users. 3) **Microsoft 365 Group** — the richest option. Creates a shared mailbox, SharePoint site, Planner board, OneNote, and Teams integration. Best for project teams or departments. Create in admin center or Teams. Choose between Public (anyone can join) and Private (invite only). Each has different use cases — distribution for one-way broadcasting, shared mailbox for team email management, M365 Group for full collaboration.
What is CI/CD and why is it important?

CI/CD automates the process of building, testing, and deploying software:

**CI (Continuous Integration)**:
- Developers merge code to a shared branch frequently (at least daily).
- Each merge triggers an automated build and test pipeline.
- Catches bugs early — when the code is fresh in the developer's mind.
- Tools: GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Jenkins, Azure DevOps Pipelines.

**CD (Continuous Delivery/Deployment)**:
- **Continuous Delivery**: Code is always in a deployable state. Deployment to production is a manual decision.
- **Continuous Deployment**: Every change that passes tests is automatically deployed to production.

**Typical pipeline**:
1. Developer pushes code to Git.
2. CI server detects the change.
3. **Build**: Compile code, install dependencies.
4. **Test**: Run unit tests, integration tests, linting.
5. **Scan**: Security vulnerability scanning, code quality checks.
6. **Package**: Create a container image or artifact.
7. **Deploy to staging**: Automated deployment to a staging environment.
8. **Deploy to production**: Automatic (CD) or after approval (Delivery).

**GitHub Actions example** (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`):
```yaml
name: CI
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '20'
      - run: npm install
      - run: npm test
      - run: npm run build
```

**Why IT support should care**:
- Understanding CI/CD helps troubleshoot deployment issues.
- Build agents/runners need infrastructure support.
- Pipeline failures are often environment issues (missing dependencies, permissions, network).
- Log analysis and debugging skills apply directly.
What are the different types of load balancing?

Load balancing distributes network traffic across multiple servers:

**Algorithms**:
1. **Round Robin**: Requests go to each server in turn (1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3...). Simple but doesn't account for server load.
2. **Weighted Round Robin**: Servers with higher weight get more requests. Good when servers have different capacities.
3. **Least Connections**: Sends traffic to the server with the fewest active connections. Good for long-lived connections.
4. **IP Hash**: Client IP determines which server handles the request. Ensures a client always reaches the same server (sticky sessions).
5. **Random**: Random server selection. Surprisingly effective at scale.
6. **Health-based**: Routes only to healthy servers. Combined with other algorithms.

**Layer 4 vs Layer 7**:
- **Layer 4 (Transport)**: Routes based on IP and port. Faster, less CPU. Can't inspect HTTP content.
- **Layer 7 (Application)**: Routes based on HTTP headers, URLs, cookies. More intelligent but more resource-intensive.
  - Example: Route `/api/*` to API servers, `/static/*` to CDN.

**Types of load balancers**:
- **Hardware**: F5 BIG-IP, Citrix ADC. Expensive but powerful.
- **Software**: Nginx, HAProxy, Traefik. Flexible and cost-effective.
- **Cloud**: AWS ALB/NLB, Azure Load Balancer, GCP Load Balancer. Managed, scalable.
- **DNS-based**: Route 53, Cloudflare. Distribute at the DNS level.

**Health checks**: The load balancer periodically checks backend servers (HTTP GET /health). If a server fails, it's removed from the pool until it recovers.

**Session persistence**: Some apps need the same user to reach the same server (e.g., shopping cart). Use cookie-based or IP-based sticky sessions. Better approach: make apps stateless and store session data in Redis/database.
How do I add an exclusion in Windows Defender?

Sometimes Defender flags legitimate files (false positives). To exclude them:

1. **GUI**: Open Windows Security → Virus & threat protection → Manage settings (under 'Virus & threat protection settings') → scroll to 'Exclusions' → Add or remove exclusions → Add an exclusion.
2. **Exclusion types**: You can exclude a file, folder, file type (.iso, .vhd), or process (by name or path).
3. **PowerShell**:
   ```powershell
   # Exclude a folder
   Add-MpPreference -ExclusionPath 'C:\Development'
   # Exclude a file type
   Add-MpPreference -ExclusionExtension '.iso'
   # Exclude a process
   Add-MpPreference -ExclusionProcess 'devenv.exe'
   # View current exclusions
   Get-MpPreference | Select ExclusionPath, ExclusionExtension, ExclusionProcess
   ```
4. **Group Policy**: Computer Configuration → Administrative Templates → Windows Components → Microsoft Defender Antivirus → Exclusions.

**Security warning**: Only exclude files/folders you trust. Excluding entire drives or user profiles significantly reduces your protection.
Explain the concept of ITIL and its key processes for IT service management.

**ITIL (Information Technology Infrastructure Library)** is a framework of best practices for delivering IT services. ITIL 4 (current version) focuses on creating value through IT services.

**Key ITIL practices**:

**1. Incident Management**:
- Goal: restore normal service operation as quickly as possible.
- Process: detection → logging → categorization → prioritization → investigation → resolution → closure.
- Major incident process for critical outages (separate from normal incident flow).

**2. Problem Management**:
- Goal: prevent incidents by identifying and resolving root causes.
- Reactive: investigate recurring incidents to find root causes.
- Proactive: identify potential problems before they cause incidents.
- Known Error Database (KEDB): documented workarounds for known issues.

**3. Change Management (Change Enablement)**:
- Goal: ensure changes are made with minimal risk and disruption.
- Types: standard (pre-approved, low risk), normal (requires assessment and approval), emergency (expedited for critical fixes).
- Change Advisory Board (CAB) reviews and approves normal changes.

**4. Service Request Management**:
- Handles predefined, pre-approved user requests: password resets, software installs, access requests.
- Different from incidents (something broken) or changes (infrastructure modification).

**5. Service Level Management**:
- Defines and monitors SLAs (Service Level Agreements) with the business.
- Example SLA: 'Email service will be available 99.9% of the time with <4 hour resolution for P1 incidents.'

**6. Knowledge Management**:
- Captures and shares knowledge to improve efficiency.
- Maintains a Knowledge Base for self-service and technician reference.

**For IT support professionals**: understanding ITIL vocabulary (incident vs. problem vs. change, SLA, CMDB) is expected in most enterprise environments. Many organizations are ITIL-aligned even if they don't follow it strictly.
How do I assign a Microsoft 365 license to a user?

You can assign licenses through the admin center or PowerShell:

**Admin Center**:
1. Go to admin.microsoft.com.
2. Users → Active users → select the user.
3. Licenses and apps tab → check the license you want to assign (e.g., Microsoft 365 Business Standard).
4. Expand the license to enable/disable specific apps (Exchange, Teams, SharePoint, etc.).
5. Click Save changes.

**Bulk assignment**:
1. Users → Active users → select multiple users (checkboxes).
2. Click 'Manage product licenses' → Replace/Add → select the license → Save.

**PowerShell** (Microsoft Graph module):
```powershell
# Connect
Connect-MgGraph -Scopes 'User.ReadWrite.All','Organization.Read.All'

# Get available licenses (SKU IDs)
Get-MgSubscribedSku | Select SkuPartNumber, SkuId, ConsumedUnits, @{N='Available';E={$_.PrepaidUnits.Enabled - $_.ConsumedUnits}}

# Assign a license
Set-MgUserLicense -UserId 'user@company.com' -AddLicenses @{SkuId='<sku-guid>'} -RemoveLicenses @()

# Remove a license
Set-MgUserLicense -UserId 'user@company.com' -AddLicenses @() -RemoveLicenses @('<sku-guid>')
```

**Group-based licensing** (recommended for scale):
1. Create a security group in Azure AD/Entra ID.
2. Go to the group → Licenses → + Assignments → select the license → Save.
3. Add users to the group — they automatically get the license.
4. Remove from group = license removed.

**Note**: You need available licenses (paid seats) to assign. Check Billing → Your products for license counts.
How do I reset a user's password in Active Directory?

You need the Active Directory Users and Computers tool (ADUC) and the right permissions.

**Using the GUI:**
1. Open Active Directory Users and Computers (dsa.msc).
2. Find the user: Right-click your domain > Find. Type their name and click Find Now.
3. Right-click the user > Reset Password.
4. Type the new temporary password. Check 'User must change password at next logon'. Click OK.
5. If the account is also locked, check 'Unlock the user's account' in the same dialog.

**Using PowerShell (faster):**
```
# Reset password and force change at next login
Set-ADAccountPassword -Identity jsmith -Reset -NewPassword (ConvertTo-SecureString 'TempPass123!' -AsPlainText -Force)
Set-ADUser -Identity jsmith -ChangePasswordAtLogon $true

# Unlock the account if locked
Unlock-ADAccount -Identity jsmith
```

⚠ Always use a temporary password and force the user to change it. Never set their permanent password for them.
A user says they can't open PDF files — they get an error or the wrong program opens. How do I fix this?

Fix PDF file association issues: 1) **Set the default PDF reader** — right-click any PDF file → Open with → Choose another app → select the preferred reader (Adobe Acrobat, Edge, Chrome) → check 'Always use this app to open .pdf files'. Or: Settings → Apps → Default apps → search '.pdf' → select the preferred reader. 2) **If no PDF reader is installed** — install Adobe Acrobat Reader DC from the official Adobe website, or use the built-in Microsoft Edge (which handles PDFs natively). 3) **If Adobe Reader crashes on open**: a) Repair the installation: Help → Repair Installation. b) Clear the Adobe cache: delete contents of %AppData%\Adobe\ and %LocalAppData%\Adobe\. c) Uninstall and reinstall the latest version. d) Try disabling Protected Mode: Edit → Preferences → Security (Enhanced) → uncheck 'Enable Protected Mode at startup'. 4) **If the PDF itself is corrupt** — try opening it in a different reader (Edge, Chrome, Firefox). If all fail, the file may be damaged. Ask the sender to resend it. 5) **Group Policy** — in enterprise environments, deploy the default PDF association via GPO: Computer Configuration → Preferences → Control Panel Settings → Folder Options → New → file type → extension .pdf → set the program.
How do I set up a PXE boot server for OS deployment?

PXE (Preboot Execution Environment) allows booting and installing an OS over the network.

**Components needed:**
• DHCP server (to direct clients to the PXE server).
• TFTP server (serves boot files).
• HTTP/SMB server (serves the OS installation files).

**Linux PXE server setup:**
```bash
# Install packages
sudo apt install tftpd-hpa isc-dhcp-server apache2 syslinux pxelinux

# Configure TFTP
sudo cp /usr/lib/PXELINUX/pxelinux.0 /srv/tftp/
sudo cp /usr/lib/syslinux/modules/bios/ldlinux.c32 /srv/tftp/
sudo mkdir -p /srv/tftp/pxelinux.cfg

# Create boot menu
cat > /srv/tftp/pxelinux.cfg/default << 'EOF'
DEFAULT menu.c32
PROMPT 0
MENU TITLE PXE Boot Menu

LABEL ubuntu
  MENU LABEL Install Ubuntu 22.04
  KERNEL ubuntu/vmlinuz
  APPEND initrd=ubuntu/initrd vga=normal

LABEL local
  MENU LABEL Boot from local disk
  LOCALBOOT 0
EOF
```

**DHCP config** (`/etc/dhcp/dhcpd.conf`):
```
subnet 10.0.1.0 netmask 255.255.255.0 {
  range 10.0.1.100 10.0.1.200;
  option routers 10.0.1.1;
  next-server 10.0.1.10;          # PXE server IP
  filename "pxelinux.0";           # Boot file
}
```

**Windows deployment**: use Windows Deployment Services (WDS) or Microsoft Deployment Toolkit (MDT) instead — they include PXE, image management, and task sequences.
How do I use Python to monitor system resources?

The `psutil` library provides cross-platform system monitoring.

```python
import psutil
import datetime

# CPU
print(f'CPU Usage: {psutil.cpu_percent(interval=1)}%')
print(f'CPU Count: {psutil.cpu_count()} cores')

# Memory
mem = psutil.virtual_memory()
print(f'RAM: {mem.used / 1e9:.1f}/{mem.total / 1e9:.1f} GB ({mem.percent}%)')

# Disk
for part in psutil.disk_partitions():
    usage = psutil.disk_usage(part.mountpoint)
    print(f'{part.mountpoint}: {usage.percent}% used')

# Network
net = psutil.net_io_counters()
print(f'Sent: {net.bytes_sent / 1e9:.2f} GB, Recv: {net.bytes_recv / 1e9:.2f} GB')

# Top processes by memory
procs = [(p.info['name'], p.info['memory_percent'])
         for p in psutil.process_iter(['name', 'memory_percent'])]
for name, mem_pct in sorted(procs, key=lambda x: x[1] or 0, reverse=True)[:10]:
    print(f'{name}: {mem_pct:.1f}%')

# Uptime
boot = datetime.datetime.fromtimestamp(psutil.boot_time())
print(f'Uptime: {datetime.datetime.now() - boot}')
```

Install: `pip install psutil`. Works on Windows, macOS, and Linux.
What is WSUS and how does it help manage Windows updates in an enterprise?

Windows Server Update Services (WSUS) is a free Microsoft tool that lets IT control which Windows updates are deployed to computers in the organization. Instead of each PC downloading updates directly from Microsoft (consuming internet bandwidth), WSUS downloads updates once and distributes them internally. Setup: install the WSUS role on a Windows Server. Configure products (Windows 10, Windows 11, Office) and classifications (Security Updates, Critical Updates, Feature Packs) to synchronize. Configure computers via GPO to point to the WSUS server: Computer Configuration → Administrative Templates → Windows Components → Windows Update → 'Specify intranet Microsoft update service location'. Workflow: WSUS syncs with Microsoft Update on schedule. IT reviews available updates, tests on a pilot group, then approves for deployment to production groups. Computer groups: create groups (Pilot, Workstations, Servers) to stagger deployments. Reporting: WSUS console shows compliance status per computer and update. Limitations: WSUS doesn't manage non-Microsoft updates, the interface is dated, and it requires maintenance (disk cleanup, index rebuilding). Modern alternative: Windows Update for Business + Intune for cloud-native update management with update rings, feature update deferrals, and compliance reporting.
How do I configure and troubleshoot a site-to-site VPN between two office locations?

A site-to-site VPN creates an encrypted tunnel between two firewalls/routers so both LANs can communicate. Setup overview: 1) Define the parameters on both ends—matching IKE (Phase 1) settings: encryption (AES-256), hashing (SHA-256), DH group (14 or higher), authentication (pre-shared key or certificates), lifetime. 2) Configure IPsec (Phase 2): encryption, hashing, PFS group, lifetime, and interesting traffic (which subnets can communicate). 3) Ensure both sides have static public IPs or use Dynamic DNS. 4) Open UDP 500 (IKE) and UDP 4500 (NAT-T) on any intermediate firewalls. 5) Ensure LAN subnets don't overlap (a common mistake). Troubleshooting: Check Phase 1 first—mismatched parameters here prevent any tunnel. Use 'show crypto isakmp sa' (Cisco) or VPN logs to verify. If Phase 1 is up but Phase 2 fails, check interesting traffic definitions and IPsec parameters. If the tunnel is up but traffic doesn't flow, check routing tables and firewall rules allowing traffic through the tunnel interface.
A user clicked on a phishing link and entered their password. What steps should I take immediately?

Act quickly — this is an incident response situation: 1) **Reset the password immediately** — in Azure AD/Active Directory, force a password reset and select 'Sign out of all sessions'. 2) **Revoke all active tokens** — in Azure AD: Users → select user → Revoke sessions. This forces re-authentication on all devices. 3) **Enable/verify MFA** — if not already enabled, enable it now. If enabled, check the MFA methods haven't been tampered with. 4) **Check sign-in logs** — Azure AD → Sign-in logs. Look for logins from unusual locations, IP addresses, or devices. 5) **Check mailbox rules** — in Exchange admin center, look for forwarding rules or inbox rules that the attacker may have created to redirect email. 6) **Scan for lateral movement** — check if the account was used to access SharePoint, Teams, or other resources suspiciously. 7) **Report the phishing email** — submit it to Microsoft (Report Message add-in) and block the sender. 8) **Document the incident** per your incident response plan and notify your security team.
How do I use Windows Deployment Services (WDS) for imaging?

WDS deploys Windows images over the network via PXE.

**Setup:**
```powershell
# Install WDS role
Install-WindowsFeature WDS -IncludeManagementTools

# Initialize WDS
wdsutil /initialize-server /remoteinstall:D:\RemoteInstall /authorize
```

**Configuration:**
1. Open WDS management console.
2. Add a boot image: use `boot.wim` from a Windows installation media.
3. Add an install image: use `install.wim` (or a captured custom image).
4. Configure PXE response: respond to known/unknown clients.

**Capture a reference image:**
1. Build a reference PC with desired OS, updates, and software.
2. Run Sysprep: `sysprep /generalize /oobe /shutdown`
3. PXE boot the reference PC.
4. Choose 'Capture Image' from the boot menu.
5. Upload to WDS as a new install image.

**MDT (Microsoft Deployment Toolkit) integration:**
• MDT adds task sequences — automated steps for OS deployment.
• Task sequence: format disk → install OS → install drivers → install software → join domain → run scripts.
• LiteTouchInstallation — minimal user interaction during deployment.

**Modern alternative:**
• Windows Autopilot — cloud-based, zero-touch provisioning.
• Ship laptops directly to users — they sign in, Intune configures everything.
• No imaging needed — vendor installs stock Windows, Autopilot customizes it.
A user left the company and we need to preserve their mailbox data. What are our options in Microsoft 365?

Several approaches depending on retention needs: 1) Convert to shared mailbox (free, no license needed)—the mailbox stays accessible to designated users. This is the most common approach. In Exchange Admin Center → Recipients → Mailboxes → select user → Convert to shared mailbox. 2) Place a Litigation Hold or In-Place Hold before deleting the account—this preserves all mailbox content including deleted items. 3) Export to PST using eDiscovery: Compliance Center → Content Search → search the user's mailbox → export results as PST. 4) Set up email forwarding to their manager before removing the account. 5) For inactive mailboxes: apply a hold, then delete the account—the mailbox becomes an 'inactive mailbox' retained for the hold duration. Best practice: Convert to shared mailbox, grant access to the manager, set up auto-reply informing senders, and keep for 90 days before archiving.

How do I implement single sign-on (SSO) for web applications?

SSO lets users access multiple applications with one set of credentials.

**Protocols:**
• **SAML 2.0**: XML-based, widely supported by enterprise apps.
• **OAuth 2.0 + OIDC**: modern, JSON-based, better for APIs and mobile.
• **WS-Federation**: older Microsoft protocol (ADFS).

**How SAML SSO works:**
1. User visits app (Service Provider).
2. App redirects to Identity Provider (IdP) — e.g., Azure AD.
3. User authenticates at IdP (if not already signed in).
4. IdP sends SAML assertion (signed XML) back to app.
5. App validates assertion and creates a session.

**Azure AD SSO setup:**
1. Entra Admin Center → Enterprise Applications → New Application.
2. Find the app in the gallery (or add custom).
3. Configure SAML:
   - Identifier (Entity ID): provided by the app.
   - Reply URL (ACS URL): where the app receives the SAML response.
   - Sign-on URL: where users go to access the app.
4. Download the Federation Metadata XML or certificate.
5. Upload to the application's SSO configuration page.
6. Assign users/groups.
7. Test SSO with the 'Test' button.

**Common issues:**
• Certificate mismatch — re-download and re-upload.
• Clock skew — SAML requires clocks to be in sync (< 5 min).
• Attribute mapping — app expects specific claim names.
• Reply URL mismatch — must be exactly right (including trailing slash).

SSO reduces password fatigue, improves security, and simplifies offboarding.
How do I troubleshoot slow Mac performance?

Step-by-step Mac performance troubleshooting:

**1. Check Activity Monitor** (Applications → Utilities):
• CPU tab: sort by CPU% — is any process using >100%?
• Memory tab: check Memory Pressure graph (green = good, yellow = OK, red = low).
• Energy tab: find battery-draining apps.

**2. Free up storage:**
• Apple  → About This Mac → Storage → Manage.
• Enable 'Optimize Storage' to offload old files to iCloud.
• Empty Trash, clear Downloads folder.
• Remove unused apps.

**3. Reduce startup items:**
• System Settings → General → Login Items.
• Remove unnecessary apps that launch at startup.

**4. Reset SMC** (Intel Macs):
• Shut down → hold Shift+Ctrl+Option+Power for 10 seconds → release → power on.
• Apple Silicon Macs: just restart (no SMC reset needed).

**5. Reset NVRAM/PRAM** (Intel):
• Restart → hold Cmd+Option+P+R for 20 seconds.

**6. Check for malware:**
• Update macOS (includes XProtect updates).
• Run Malwarebytes for Mac (free scan).

**7. If still slow:**
• Boot in Safe Mode (hold Shift at startup) — if fast in Safe Mode, a login item or extension is the problem.
• Consider upgrading RAM (if possible) or switching to SSD.
• Reinstall macOS (keeps files) via Recovery Mode.
How do I monitor AWS resources with CloudWatch?

Amazon CloudWatch collects metrics, logs, and alarms for AWS resources.

1. **Metrics**: CPU, memory, disk, network for EC2; request count for ALB; invocations for Lambda. View in Console → CloudWatch → Metrics.
2. **Alarms**: set thresholds — e.g., CPU > 80% for 5 minutes → send SNS notification or trigger Auto Scaling.
3. **Logs**: install the CloudWatch agent on EC2 to ship /var/log/syslog, application logs, etc.
4. **Dashboards**: build custom views with graphs of key metrics.

Install the agent:
```
sudo yum install amazon-cloudwatch-agent
sudo /opt/aws/amazon-cloudwatch-agent/bin/amazon-cloudwatch-agent-config-wizard
sudo systemctl start amazon-cloudwatch-agent
```

For cost awareness, CloudWatch basic metrics are free; detailed (1-minute) metrics and custom metrics cost extra.
How do I use Group Policy Preferences to map network drives?

Group Policy Preferences (GPP) provides a flexible way to map network drives for users.

**Creating the preference** (User Configuration → Preferences → Windows Settings → Drive Maps):

1. Right-click → New → Mapped Drive.
2. **Action**: choose wisely:
   - **Create**: creates the mapping only if it doesn't exist. Won't update if the path changes.
   - **Replace**: deletes and recreates the mapping every time. Ensures the current settings are applied.
   - **Update**: creates if new, updates if existing. Most flexible – recommended for most scenarios.
   - **Delete**: removes the mapping.

3. **Location**: `\\fileserver\sharename`
4. **Drive Letter**: select a specific letter or 'Use first available.'

What is SCCM/MECM and how is it used in enterprise environments?

**SCCM** (System Center Configuration Manager), now called **MECM** (Microsoft Endpoint Configuration Manager) and part of **Microsoft Intune** family, is Microsoft's enterprise endpoint management platform.

**Core capabilities**:

1. **OS Deployment (OSD)** – deploy Windows to bare-metal machines or reimage existing ones using task sequences. Supports PXE boot, USB media, and multicast. Integrates with MDT for enhanced task sequences.

2. **Software Distribution** – package and deploy applications to thousands of endpoints. Supports MSI, EXE, MSIX, and script-based installers. Features include deployment scheduling, maintenance windows, user self-service (Software Center), and approval workflows.

3. **Patch Management** – integrates with WSUS to distribute Windows updates, Microsoft 365 updates, and third-party patches. Supports deployment rings, compliance reporting, and automatic deployment rules (ADRs).

4. **Inventory and Reporting** – collects hardware inventory (CPU, RAM, disk, serial numbers) and software inventory (installed applications). SQL Reporting Services provides detailed reports for compliance and asset management.

5. **Compliance Settings** – check endpoints against baselines (e.g., BitLocker enabled, firewall on, specific registry values). Remediate non-compliant devices automatically.

6. **Endpoint Protection** – manage Windows Defender Antivirus policies, definition updates, and scan schedules.

**Architecture**: site server (primary), management points (client communication), distribution points (content delivery), SQL Server database, reporting services point, software update point (WSUS).

**Co-management with Intune**: MECM and Intune can co-manage devices – some workloads handled by MECM (on-prem), others by Intune (cloud). This is the recommended path for modernizing endpoint management.

What is the difference between a full backup, incremental backup, and differential backup?

These three backup types offer different trade-offs between backup speed, storage usage, and restore complexity. Full backup: copies ALL selected data every time it runs. Advantages: simplest to restore — only one backup set needed. Self-contained, each backup is independent. Disadvantages: slowest to perform, uses the most storage space, highest network bandwidth. Typically run weekly. Incremental backup: copies only data that has CHANGED since the LAST backup of ANY type (full or incremental). Monday full → Tuesday incremental (changes since Monday) → Wednesday incremental (changes since Tuesday only). Advantages: fastest backup, uses least storage per backup job. Disadvantages: restoration requires the last full backup PLUS every subsequent incremental in sequence — if any incremental in the chain is corrupt, all later data is lost. Slower restore time. Differential backup: copies all data that has changed since the LAST FULL backup. Monday full → Tuesday differential (changes since Monday) → Wednesday differential (ALL changes since Monday). Advantages: restore requires only the last full backup plus the latest differential — simpler and faster than incremental. Disadvantages: differential backups grow larger each day as they accumulate all changes since the last full. Takes more storage and time than incremental but less than full. Common enterprise strategy: full backup weekly (Sunday night), daily differentials (weekdays) — this provides a balance of backup speed, storage, and restore simplicity with a maximum restore of two backup sets. For critical systems with RPO near zero, consider continuous data protection (CDP) which captures every change in real-time.

What is the best way to document and hand over IT knowledge when transitioning to a new role?

How do I troubleshoot SQL Server connection issues?

**1. Is SQL Server running?**
```cmd
:: Check service
sc query MSSQLSERVER       :: Default instance
sc query MSSQL$INSTANCENAME :: Named instance
:: Or in PowerShell
Get-Service MSSQL*
```

**2. Is it listening on the right port?**
```cmd
netstat -an | findstr 1433
```
Default port is TCP 1433. Named instances use dynamic ports — check SQL Server Configuration Manager.

**3. Can you reach it from the client?**
```powershell
Test-NetConnection -ComputerName SQLSERVER -Port 1433
```

**4. Firewall open?**
```powershell
New-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName 'SQL Server' -Direction Inbound -LocalPort 1433 -Protocol TCP -Action Allow
```

**5. SQL Server Configuration Manager checks**:
- TCP/IP enabled? (SQL Server Network Configuration → Protocols → TCP/IP → Enabled).
- SQL Browser service running? (Required for named instances).
- Named Pipes enabled if needed.

**6. Authentication mode**:
- Windows Authentication only? → SA account won't work.
- Mixed mode? → Both Windows and SQL accounts work.
- Change in SSMS: Right-click server → Properties → Security → Server authentication.

**7. Connection string format**:
```
:: Default instance
Server=SERVERNAME;Database=MyDB;Trusted_Connection=True;
:: Named instance
Server=SERVERNAME\INSTANCENAME;Database=MyDB;
:: With port
Server=SERVERNAME,1433;Database=MyDB;
```

**8. SQL Server error log**:
```sql
EXEC xp_readerrorlog 0, 1, N'error'
```
Or check: `C:\Program Files\Microsoft SQL Server\MSSQLXX\MSSQL\Log\ERRORLOG`

- Error 18456: Login failed (wrong credentials or account disabled).

What is Windows Server Failover Clustering?

Failover Clustering provides high availability by grouping servers together:

**How it works**: Multiple servers (nodes) share workloads. If one node fails, another automatically takes over — this is called **failover**. The transition is often seamless to end users.

**Prerequisites**:
- Windows Server Datacenter or Standard edition.
- Identical or similar hardware across nodes.
- Shared storage (SAN, iSCSI, Storage Spaces Direct, or Azure shared disks).
- At least 2 network connections per node.
- All nodes in the same AD domain.

**Common clustered workloads**:
- **Hyper-V**: Live migration of VMs between nodes.
- **SQL Server AlwaysOn**: Database failover.
- **File Server**: Continuously available file shares.
- **DHCP**: Failover DHCP scopes.

**Setup**:
```powershell
# Install feature on all nodes
Install-WindowsFeature Failover-Clustering -IncludeManagementTools

# Validate configuration (run before creating cluster)
Test-Cluster -Node Server1,Server2 -Include Storage,Network,Inventory

# Create the cluster
New-Cluster -Name 'MyCluster' -Node Server1,Server2 -StaticAddress 10.0.1.100

# Add a role (e.g., File Server)
Add-ClusterFileServerRole -Name 'FS-Cluster' -Storage 'Cluster Disk 1' -StaticAddress 10.0.1.101
```

**Quorum**: Determines how many node failures the cluster can survive. Options:
- Node Majority: Odd number of nodes.
- Node + Disk Witness: Uses a small shared disk as a tiebreaker.
- Node + Cloud Witness: Uses Azure Blob Storage as witness (recommended for modern setups).

**Monitoring**: Failover Cluster Manager GUI, or `Get-ClusterNode`, `Get-ClusterGroup`, `Get-ClusterResource` in PowerShell.
How do I troubleshoot Group Policy Preferences drive mapping that isn't working?

GPP drive maps fail silently, making troubleshooting tricky. Steps: 1) Verify the GPO applies: 'gpresult /H report.html'. Open the report and look under User Configuration → Group Policy Preferences → Drive Maps. If it shows 'Denied' or isn't listed, check GPO link, security filtering, and WMI filters. 2) Check item-level targeting: if the drive map uses item-level targeting (e.g., 'apply only to users in the Finance security group'), verify the user meets ALL conditions. Common mistake: targeting by OU path when users have moved to a different OU. 3) Check the action type: Create (only creates if the mapping doesn't exist), Delete (removes the mapping), Replace (deletes then creates), Update (modifies existing or creates if missing). Use 'Update' for most scenarios—it's the most flexible. 4) Check credentials: GPP used to support stored credentials, but this was disabled due to the ms14-025 vulnerability (credentials were easily decrypted). If the mapping requires different credentials, it won't work with GPP—use a logon script instead. 5) Drive letter conflict: if the letter is already in use by another mapping, the preference fails. 6) Check Event Viewer: Applications and Services Logs → Microsoft → Windows → GroupPolicy → Operational. Filter for Event IDs 4016 (success) and 4098 (failure)—the failure event usually includes the specific error code and reason. 7) Run 'gpupdate /force' and log off/log on (drive maps apply at logon, not during gpupdate).
What should be included in a standard IT documentation template for systems?

Keep this template in a wiki or SharePoint and update it whenever changes are made.
How do I check disk space on Linux and find large files?

Several commands help you find what's using your disk.

**Check overall disk usage:**
```bash
df -h
```
`-h` gives human-readable sizes (GB, MB instead of blocks).

**Check directory sizes:**
```bash
du -sh /var/log
du -sh /*
```
`-s` gives a summary (total), `-h` human-readable.

**Find the biggest directories:**
```bash
du -h --max-depth=1 / | sort -rh | head -20
```
This shows the 20 largest top-level directories.

**Find large files:**
```bash
# Files over 100 MB
find / -type f -size +100M -exec ls -lh {} \; 2>/dev/null

# Top 20 largest files
find / -type f -exec du -h {} + 2>/dev/null | sort -rh | head -20
```

**Common space hogs on Linux:**
- `/var/log` — Log files can grow huge. Check with `ls -lhS /var/log`. Clean old logs: `sudo journalctl --vacuum-time=7d`
- `/tmp` — Temporary files. Safe to clear: `sudo rm -rf /tmp/*`
- Old kernel packages (Ubuntu): `sudo apt autoremove`
- Docker images: `docker system prune -a`
- Package cache: `sudo apt clean` (Ubuntu) or `sudo yum clean all` (RHEL)

**Set up alerts:**
```bash
# Simple check you can put in a cron job
if [ $(df / | tail -1 | awk '{print $5}' | tr -d '%') -gt 90 ]; then echo 'Disk over 90%'; fi
```
What is the principle of least privilege and how do you implement it in an IT environment?

The principle of least privilege (PoLP) states that users, applications, and systems should have only the minimum permissions necessary to perform their specific tasks — nothing more. Implementation across IT: Active Directory: Don't add users to Domain Admins for routine tasks. Create role-based security groups (e.g., Helpdesk-PasswordReset, Server-RDP-Access) with specific delegated permissions. Use fine-grained password policies. Implement a tiered administration model: Tier 0 (DC admins), Tier 1 (server admins), Tier 2 (workstation admins) — never use Tier 0 credentials on lower tiers. Endpoints: Remove local admin rights from standard users. Use tools like LAPS (Local Administrator Password Solution) for unique local admin passwords. Implement application whitelisting (AppLocker, Windows Defender Application Control). Cloud: Use IAM roles with specific policies instead of broad admin access. Implement just-in-time (JIT) access with Azure PIM (Privileged Identity Management) or AWS IAM Access Analyzer. Never use root/global admin accounts for daily tasks. Applications: Service accounts should run with minimal permissions. Database users should have access only to required tables/views. API keys should be scoped to needed endpoints. Network: Segment networks so users only access their segment. Use firewall rules defaulting to deny-all with explicit allows. Monitoring: implement privileged access monitoring (PAM) to log all admin actions, and regularly review access with access certifications.

What's the difference between VMware vSphere, ESXi, and vCenter?

These terms are often confused. Here's the relationship:

**ESXi** – the bare-metal hypervisor installed directly on server hardware. It's the foundation that runs virtual machines. Each physical server runs one instance of ESXi. It has a direct console (DCUI) and can be managed individually via the ESXi Host Client (web-based).

**vCenter Server** – the centralized management platform for multiple ESXi hosts. It provides:
- Single pane of glass management for all hosts and VMs.
- vMotion (live migration of running VMs between hosts).
- DRS (Distributed Resource Scheduler) – automatic load balancing.
- HA (High Availability) – restarts VMs on surviving hosts if a host fails.
- Distributed switches, storage DRS, host profiles.
- Role-based access control, licensing management.
- Deployed as a virtual appliance (VCSA – vCenter Server Appliance) running Photon OS.

**vSphere** – the product suite that includes ESXi + vCenter + the vSphere Client (web interface). It's the brand name for VMware's entire server virtualization platform. When someone says 'we run vSphere,' they mean ESXi on their servers managed by vCenter.

**Analogy**: ESXi is like an individual worker, vCenter is the manager overseeing the team, and vSphere is the name of the company/department.

**Licensing**: ESXi is licensed per CPU. vCenter has its own license (Standard or Foundation). vSphere editions (Standard, Enterprise Plus) bundle ESXi and vCenter licenses with different feature sets.

**You can run ESXi without vCenter** for small environments (1-2 hosts), but you lose all the advanced features (vMotion, HA, DRS). For production environments, vCenter is essential.
How do I configure NAT (Network Address Translation) on a router?

NAT translates private IPs to public IPs for internet access: 1) **PAT/NAT Overload** (most common — many private IPs share one public IP): On Cisco: 'ip nat inside source list 1 interface GigabitEthernet0/0 overload', where access-list 1 defines which internal networks: 'access-list 1 permit 192.168.1.0 0.0.0.255'. Mark interfaces: 'interface GigabitEthernet0/1' (LAN) → 'ip nat inside', 'interface GigabitEthernet0/0' (WAN) → 'ip nat outside'. 2) **Static NAT** (maps one private IP to one public IP — for servers): 'ip nat inside source static 192.168.1.100 203.0.113.10'. Use this when external systems need to reach an internal server. 3) **Port forwarding** (static NAT for specific ports): 'ip nat inside source static tcp 192.168.1.100 443 203.0.113.10 443'. Only forwards HTTPS traffic to the internal server. 4) **Verify**: 'show ip nat translations' shows active translations. 'show ip nat statistics' shows translation counts. 5) **Troubleshoot**: 'debug ip nat' (use carefully in production). Common issues: missing inside/outside interface designations, incorrect ACL not matching the right subnets, or NAT and routing conflicts. 6) **On Linux**: Use iptables: 'iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -o eth0 -j MASQUERADE' for PAT, or 'iptables -t nat -A PREROUTING -p tcp --dport 443 -j DNAT --to-destination 192.168.1.100:443' for port forwarding.
What is a service mesh and when would you use one?

A service mesh is a dedicated infrastructure layer that handles service-to-service communication in a microservices architecture. Instead of each microservice implementing its own networking logic (retries, timeouts, encryption, load balancing), the service mesh provides these features transparently through sidecar proxies deployed alongside each service. How it works: a sidecar proxy (typically Envoy) is injected alongside each service pod in Kubernetes. All traffic in and out of the service goes through this proxy. A control plane (like Istio's istiod) configures all the proxies centrally. Key capabilities: Traffic management — canary deployments (route 5% of traffic to new version), A/B testing, circuit breaking (stop sending traffic to failing services), retries with backoff, rate limiting. Security — mutual TLS (mTLS) between all services automatically, fine-grained access policies (service A can call service B but not service C). Observability — distributed tracing (Jaeger, Zipkin integration), metrics (latency, error rates, request volumes), service dependency graphs. Popular service meshes: Istio (most feature-rich, Kubernetes-native), Linkerd (lightweight, easier to operate), Consul Connect (HashiCorp, multi-platform). When to use: when you have many microservices (20+) that need consistent security, observability, and traffic policies. Don't use for monoliths or small service counts — the complexity overhead isn't justified.

**Before editing — BACK UP**:
1. **Export specific key**: Right-click the key you're changing → Export → save as .reg file.
2. **Full backup**: File → Export → All → save to a safe location.
3. **Create a restore point**: Search 'Create a restore point' → click Create.

**Structure**:
- `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE (HKLM)`: System-wide settings.
- `HKEY_CURRENT_USER (HKCU)`: Current user settings.
- `HKEY_CLASSES_ROOT (HKCR)`: File associations and COM objects.

How do I troubleshoot DNS resolution issues on a network?

Systematic DNS troubleshooting: 1) **Verify the problem is DNS**: Can you ping by IP (ping 8.8.8.8) but not by name (ping google.com)? If IP works but name doesn't, it's DNS. If neither works, it's a network connectivity issue. 2) **Check DNS configuration**: 'ipconfig /all' — verify the DNS server IPs are correct. For domain machines, primary DNS should be your domain controller. 3) **Test DNS resolution**: 'nslookup google.com' — does it return an IP? Try 'nslookup google.com 8.8.8.8' to test against Google's DNS. If Google's works but yours doesn't, the problem is your DNS server. 4) **Flush DNS cache**: 'ipconfig /flushdns' — clears cached entries that might be stale. 5) **Check DNS server**: RDP to your DNS server, open DNS Manager, verify zones are loaded, check forwarders are configured (e.g., 8.8.8.8, 1.1.1.1). Check Event Viewer for DNS errors. 6) **Test forward and reverse lookups**: 'nslookup <hostname>' (forward) and 'nslookup <IP>' (reverse). Missing reverse lookup zones can cause delays. 7) **Clear the DNS server cache**: Open DNS Manager → right-click the server → Clear Cache. 8) **Check if a specific record is wrong**: 'nslookup -type=A hostname.domain.com' — verify the returned IP is correct.

How do I troubleshoot a Kubernetes pod stuck in ImagePullBackOff status?

ImagePullBackOff means Kubernetes can't pull the container image. Diagnose with 'kubectl describe pod <pod-name>'—look at the Events section for the specific error. Check the registry with 'docker pull <image>' from a machine with access. 2) Authentication failure—the registry requires credentials. Create a secret: 'kubectl create secret docker-registry regcred --docker-server=<registry> --docker-username=<user> --docker-password=<pass>' and reference it in the pod spec: 'imagePullSecrets: [{name: regcred}]'. 3) Private registry not accessible—check network connectivity from the nodes to the registry. 4) Tag doesn't exist—'latest' tag might have been removed. A user reports that their mapped network drive disconnects frequently. How do you troubleshoot?

Frequent network drive disconnections have several common causes. First, check the basics: verify the server hosting the share is stable and not rebooting or losing connectivity. Ping the server continuously: 'ping -t servername' to check for packet loss or latency spikes. Common fixes: 1) Disable offline files (caching): Control Panel → Sync Center → Manage Offline Files → Disable Offline Files → Restart. 2) Prevent Windows from disconnecting idle connections — by default, Windows disconnects SMB sessions after 15 minutes of inactivity. On the server: 'Set-SmbServerConfiguration -AutoDisconnectTimeout -1' (disables auto-disconnect). 3) Keep-alive settings: ensure the network adapter isn't set to power saving mode — Device Manager → Network adapter → Properties → Power Management → uncheck 'Allow the computer to turn off this device to save power'. 4) Update network drivers on both client and server. 5) If using Wi-Fi, ensure signal strength is adequate — wired connections are preferred for mapped drives. 6) Check if the issue is with credential expiry: re-map the drive with persistent flag: 'net use Z: \\server\share /persistent:yes'. 7) Verify SMB version compatibility — both client and server should support SMB3. 8) Check for Group Policy settings that might be remapping drives at logon and conflicting. 9) Review the event logs on both client and server for SMB or network errors.
How do I resize a partition on Linux without losing data?

You can resize partitions on Linux using command-line tools or GParted.

**Method 1 — GParted (GUI, easiest):**
1. Boot from a GParted live USB (you can't resize a mounted partition).
2. Select the partition you want to resize.
3. Right-click > Resize/Move.
4. Drag the edges or enter the new size.
5. Click Apply. Wait for it to finish.

**Method 2 — Command line (for extending, most common in servers):**

If you added a larger disk or expanded the VM disk:
```bash
# 1. Check current partition layout
lsblk
df -h

# 2. Extend the partition (using growpart for cloud VMs)
sudo growpart /dev/sda 1

# 3. Resize the filesystem
# For ext4:
sudo resize2fs /dev/sda1

# For XFS:
sudo xfs_growfs /
```

**For LVM (Logical Volume Manager):**
```bash
# Extend the logical volume
sudo lvextend -l +100%FREE /dev/mapper/vg-lv_root

# Resize the filesystem
sudo resize2fs /dev/mapper/vg-lv_root
# Or for XFS:
sudo xfs_growfs /dev/mapper/vg-lv_root
```

**Important notes:**
- You can grow a partition while it's mounted (for ext4 and XFS).
- Shrinking requires unmounting first and is riskier.
- Always back up before resizing partitions.
- XFS can only be grown, never shrunk.
- ext4 can be both grown and shrunk.

How do I set up a web application firewall (WAF) to protect against common attacks?

WAF deployment protects web applications: 1) **Choose a WAF**: AWS WAF (for applications behind ALB/CloudFront), Azure WAF (for Azure Application Gateway/Front Door), Cloudflare (SaaS, easy to deploy), or ModSecurity (open source, self-hosted with Nginx/Apache). 2) **Deploy in monitoring mode first**: Set the WAF to 'detect only' or 'log only' mode to identify false positives before blocking traffic. What is LDAP and how is it used in enterprise environments?

LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) is a protocol for accessing and managing directory information services over a network. It organizes data in a hierarchical tree structure (Directory Information Tree) with entries identified by Distinguished Names (DNs), like CN=John Smith,OU=Sales,DC=company,DC=com. In enterprise environments, LDAP is primarily used through Active Directory (AD) on Windows or OpenLDAP on Linux. Common uses include: centralized authentication — users log in once and access multiple services; user and group management — storing employee information, group memberships, and organizational structure; email address books — Outlook and other clients query LDAP for contact information; application authentication — web apps, VPNs, and Wi-Fi authenticate against LDAP; and access control — determining permissions based on group membership. LDAP typically runs on port 389 (unencrypted) or port 636 (LDAPS, encrypted with SSL/TLS). Always use LDAPS in production. Tools like ldapsearch, Apache Directory Studio, or AD Users and Computers are used to manage LDAP directories.

How do I set up log rotation on a Linux server?

logrotate manages log files to prevent disk space exhaustion: 1) **Global config**: /etc/logrotate.conf sets defaults. Application-specific configs go in /etc/logrotate.d/. 2) **Create a config** for your application: Create /etc/logrotate.d/myapp with: '/var/log/myapp/*.log { daily, rotate 14, compress, delaycompress, missingok, notifempty, create 0640 myapp myapp, sharedscripts, postrotate /bin/systemctl reload myapp > /dev/null 2>&1 || true, endscript }'. 3) **Key directives**: 'daily/weekly/monthly' — rotation frequency. 'rotate 14' — keep 14 rotated files. 'compress' — gzip old logs. 'delaycompress' — don't compress the most recent rotated file (useful if the app still writes to it briefly). 'missingok' — don't error if the log file doesn't exist. 'copytruncate' — copy the file and truncate the original (for apps that don't support log reopening). 'maxsize 100M' — rotate when the file exceeds 100MB regardless of schedule. 4) **Test**: 'sudo logrotate -d /etc/logrotate.d/myapp' (dry run) to see what would happen. How do I investigate a potential security breach in a Windows environment?

Structured incident investigation: 1) Contain first—isolate the affected system(s) from the network (disable NIC, VLAN isolation) to prevent lateral movement. Don't turn off the machine (preserves volatile data in memory). 2) Collect volatile data: capture RAM using tools like WinPmem or Magnet RAM Capture. Record running processes ('tasklist /v'), network connections ('netstat -anob'), logged-on users ('query user'), scheduled tasks, and services. 3) Check Event Logs (the goldmine): Security log—event IDs 4624 (logon), 4625 (failed logon), 4720 (account created), 4732 (user added to group), 4688 (process creation). System log—service installations (7045), unexpected reboots. PowerShell logs (if enabled)—script block logging shows executed commands. 4) Check for persistence: startup items (autoruns from Sysinternals), scheduled tasks, registry run keys, WMI subscriptions, services. 5) Check for lateral movement: RDP logs, PsExec usage, WMI/WinRM connections to other hosts. 6) File system analysis: recently modified files, files in temp directories, unusual executables. Use 'dir /s /od' to find recently modified files. 7) Network analysis: DNS query logs, proxy/firewall logs for C2 (command and control) communication. 8) Create a timeline correlating all evidence. 9) Document everything for potential legal proceedings. 10) After investigation, remediate: patch the vulnerability, reset affected credentials, enhance monitoring.

How do I manage Windows Event Logs for troubleshooting?

Windows Event Logs are essential for diagnosing system issues.

**Key logs:**
• **System**: hardware, drivers, services, startup/shutdown.
• **Application**: software errors, crashes.
• **Security**: logon/logoff, privilege use, policy changes.
• **Setup**: Windows Update, role installation.

**Event Viewer:**
1. Run `eventvwr.msc`.
2. Windows Logs → System (or Application, Security).
3. Filter by: level (Error, Warning), event ID, source, date range.

**Important Event IDs:**
• **41**: Unexpected shutdown (crash/power loss).
• **1074**: Clean shutdown/restart (includes who initiated it).
• **6008**: Unexpected previous shutdown.
• **7036**: Service started/stopped.
• **4624**: Successful logon.
• **4625**: Failed logon.
• **4720**: User account created.
• **4726**: User account deleted.
• **4740**: Account locked out.
• **1001**: Windows Error Reporting (application crash details).

**PowerShell queries:**
```powershell
# Last 10 errors in System log
Get-WinEvent -LogName System -MaxEvents 10 | Where-Object {$_.LevelDisplayName -eq 'Error'}

# BSOD events
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='System'; ID=41} | Select-Object TimeCreated, Message

# Failed logons in last 24 hours
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security'; ID=4625; StartTime=(Get-Date).AddDays(-1)}

# Account lockouts
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security'; ID=4740} | ForEach-Object { $_.Message }

```

How do I use Windows Performance Monitor (perfmon) to diagnose server performance issues?

Performance Monitor (perfmon.exe) is built into Windows and provides real-time and historical performance data.

**Quick overview**:
- Open `perfmon.exe` from Run dialog or search.
- The default view shows a real-time graph of % Processor Time.

**Key counters to monitor**:

**CPU**:
- `Processor\% Processor Time\_Total` – overall CPU usage. Sustained >80% indicates a bottleneck.
- `System\Processor Queue Length` – threads waiting for CPU. Should be <2× number of cores.

**Memory**:
- `Memory\Available MBytes` – free physical memory. Below 10% of total is concerning.
- `Memory\Pages/sec` – hard page faults (reading from disk). Sustained >50 indicates memory pressure.
- `Paging File\% Usage` – high usage means the system is swapping to disk.

**Disk**:
- `PhysicalDisk\% Disk Time` – how busy the disk is. Sustained >80% is a bottleneck.
- `PhysicalDisk\Avg. Disk Queue Length` – requests waiting. >2 per disk is concerning.
- `PhysicalDisk\Avg. Disk sec/Read` and `sec/Write` – latency. >20ms for SSDs or >50ms for HDDs is slow.

**Network**:
- `Network Interface\Bytes Total/sec` – compare to link speed to check saturation.
- `Network Interface\Output Queue Length` – >2 indicates network congestion.

**Creating a Data Collector Set** (for historical analysis):
1. perfmon → Data Collector Sets → User Defined → right-click → New → Data Collector Set.
2. Name it, select 'Create manually', choose Performance counter.
3. Add the counters above, set sample interval (15 seconds is good).
4. Set a stop condition (e.g., run for 24 hours).
5. Start the collection.
6. View the results under Reports → User Defined.

**Pro tip**: use `typeperf` from the command line for quick checks:
```cmd
typeperf "\Processor(_Total)\% Processor Time" "\Memory\Available MBytes" -si 5 -sc 20
```
I keep getting blue screens (BSOD). How do I diagnose the cause?

Blue Screen of Death (BSOD) diagnostics:

**Immediate info from the BSOD screen**:
- Note the stop code (e.g., IRQL_NOT_LESS_OR_EQUAL, KERNEL_DATA_INPAGE_ERROR, SYSTEM_SERVICE_EXCEPTION).
- Note the 'What failed' file if shown (e.g., ntfs.sys, nvlddmkm.sys).

**Analyze crash dumps**:
1. Crash dumps are saved to `C:\Windows\Minidump\`.
2. Download **WinDbg** (from Microsoft Store, free).
3. Open WinDbg → File → Open Crash Dump → select the .dmp file.
4. Run `!analyze -v` — this shows the faulting driver/module, stack trace, and probable cause.
5. Or use **BlueScreenView** (NirSoft, free) — it automatically reads all dump files and shows the crashing driver.

**Common stop codes and causes**:
| Stop Code | Usual Cause |
|-----------|-------------|
| IRQL_NOT_LESS_OR_EQUAL | Bad driver or RAM |
| PAGE_FAULT_IN_NONPAGED_AREA | Bad RAM or corrupted driver |
| KERNEL_DATA_INPAGE_ERROR | Failing hard drive |
| SYSTEM_SERVICE_EXCEPTION | Driver conflict or corrupted system file |
| DPC_WATCHDOG_VIOLATION | Storage driver or SSD firmware |
| VIDEO_TDR_FAILURE | GPU driver crash |

**General fixes**:
1. Update all drivers (especially GPU, chipset, storage).
2. Run `sfc /scannow` and `DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth`.
3. Test RAM with MemTest86.
4. Check disk: `chkdsk C: /f /r`.
5. Check temps — overheating causes BSODs.
6. If it started after a driver/software install, System Restore to before the install.
What is the difference between RAID 0, 1, 5, 6, and 10?

RAID (Redundant Array of Independent Disks) combines multiple drives for performance, redundancy, or both.

**RAID 0 (Striping)**:
- Data is split across all drives. No redundancy.
- **Capacity**: 100% (2×1TB = 2TB usable).
- **Performance**: excellent read/write (2x or more).
- **Fault tolerance**: NONE. One drive failure = total data loss.
- **Min drives**: 2.
- **Use case**: temporary/scratch data, video editing buffers. Never for important data.

**RAID 1 (Mirroring)**:
- Data is duplicated on two drives. Every write goes to both.
- **Capacity**: 50% (2×1TB = 1TB usable).
- **Performance**: read speed doubled, write speed same as single drive.
- **Fault tolerance**: survives 1 drive failure.
- **Min drives**: 2.
- **Use case**: OS drives, small critical data sets, boot drives.

**RAID 5 (Striping with Distributed Parity)**:
- Data and parity information are striped across all drives. Parity allows recovery from one drive failure.
- **Capacity**: (n-1) drives (3×1TB = 2TB usable).
- **Performance**: good read, slower write (parity calculation).
- **Fault tolerance**: survives 1 drive failure. During rebuild, a second failure = total loss.
- **Min drives**: 3.
- **Use case**: file servers, general-purpose storage. Falling out of favor for large drives (long rebuild times increase risk).

**RAID 6 (Striping with Double Parity)**:
- Like RAID 5 but with two parity blocks. Can survive two simultaneous drive failures.
- **Capacity**: (n-2) drives (4×1TB = 2TB usable).
- **Performance**: good read, slower write than RAID 5.
- **Fault tolerance**: survives 2 drive failures.
- **Min drives**: 4.
- **Use case**: large arrays where rebuild times are long, archives, NAS appliances.

**RAID 10 (1+0, Mirrored Stripes)**:
- Combines RAID 1 and RAID 0: data is mirrored in pairs, then striped.
- **Capacity**: 50% (4×1TB = 2TB usable).
- **Performance**: excellent read and write.
- **Fault tolerance**: survives 1 drive failure per mirrored pair (can survive multiple failures if they're in different pairs).
- **Min drives**: 4.
- **Use case**: databases, high-performance applications, VMs. The preferred RAID level for most enterprise workloads.

**Summary**: RAID 10 for performance + redundancy, RAID 6 for maximum redundancy, RAID 1 for simplicity. Avoid RAID 0 for anything important. RAID 5 is acceptable for smaller arrays with fast rebuild times.
How do I prepare for an IT audit?

Audit preparation checklist: 1) **Understand the scope** — what standard or regulation is being audited? (SOC 2, ISO 27001, PCI-DSS, HIPAA, internal policy). Request the audit scope and controls list in advance. 2) **Gather documentation**: IT policies (acceptable use, security, backup, incident response, change management), network diagrams, system inventories, user access lists, change management logs, incident reports, backup and restore test records, vendor risk assessments, training records. 3) **Review access controls**: Run Active Directory reports — who has admin access? Are there stale accounts? Are permissions based on roles (least privilege)? Clean up before the audit, not during. 4) **Verify technical controls**: Are all systems patched to current levels? Is antivirus deployed and updated on all endpoints? Are firewalls configured with deny-by-default rules? Are logs being collected and retained per policy? Are backups running and restore-tested? 5) **Prepare evidence**: Auditors want proof, not promises. Screenshots of configurations, exports of policy settings, sample change tickets showing the approval process, training completion reports. 6) **Brief your team**: Everyone who might be interviewed should understand the policies and their responsibilities. 7) **Track findings**: Use a spreadsheet or GRC tool to track audit findings, remediation actions, owners, and deadlines.
How do I implement a patch management strategy for a Windows environment?

A structured patch management process keeps systems secure while minimizing disruption.

**1. Inventory and categorize systems**:
- Classify all systems by criticality: mission-critical servers, business applications, workstations, dev/test.
- Maintain an accurate CMDB or inventory.

**2. Patch assessment** (Patch Tuesday + 1-2 days):
- Review Microsoft's monthly security bulletin.
- Prioritize based on: CVSS score, whether it's actively exploited (check CISA KEV list), which systems are affected, and whether the vulnerability is internet-facing.

**3. Testing** (Week 1):
- Deploy patches to a test/lab environment first.
- Test against critical applications for compatibility.
- Include both security updates and any optional updates being considered.

**4. Phased rollout**:
- **Ring 0 (Week 1)**: IT department workstations – canary group.
- **Ring 1 (Week 2)**: non-critical workstations and dev servers.
- **Ring 2 (Week 3)**: production workstations and low-criticality servers.
- **Ring 3 (Week 4)**: critical production servers during maintenance windows.

**5. Deployment tools**:
- **WSUS** (Windows Server Update Services): free, on-premises, good for small-medium environments.
- **SCCM/MECM**: enterprise-grade, integrates with broader endpoint management.
- **Intune**: cloud-managed, ideal for modern management and remote workers.
- **Azure Update Management**: for Azure VMs and hybrid environments.
- **Third-party**: Ivanti, ManageEngine, PDQ Deploy for non-Microsoft patches.

**6. Verification and reporting**:
- Check compliance rates: what percentage of devices are patched within SLA?
- Generate compliance reports for management and auditors.
- Address non-compliant devices: investigate why they didn't patch (offline, errors, exclusions).

**7. Emergency patching**:
- For actively-exploited zero-days, compress the timeline: test immediately and deploy within 24-48 hours.
- Have a pre-approved emergency change process.

**Metrics to track**: patch compliance rate (target >95%), mean time to patch, number of rollbacks, patch-related incidents.

What is Windows Server Update Services (WSUS) maintenance and why is it important?

WSUS requires regular maintenance or it becomes slow and unreliable. Key maintenance tasks: 1) Server Cleanup Wizard: WSUS Console → Options → Server Cleanup Wizard. Remove: unneeded updates (superseded, expired, declined), computers that haven't contacted the server in 30+ days, unneeded update files, unneeded update revisions. Run monthly. 2) Decline superseded updates: updates that have been replaced by newer ones. Either manually or with PowerShell: 'Get-WsusUpdate -Approval AnyExceptDeclined -Status Any | Where {$_.Update.IsSuperseded} | Deny-WsusUpdate'. 3) Re-index the WSUS database: the WID (Windows Internal Database) or SQL database gets fragmented. Run the Microsoft-provided maintenance SQL script monthly. This significantly improves console responsiveness. 4) IIS Application Pool recycling: WSUS Application Pool → Advanced Settings → Private Memory Limit. Set to 0 (unlimited) or a high value (8GB+) to prevent crashes during sync. Increase the queue length to 25000. 5) Disk space: WSUS can consume hundreds of GB. Only sync products and categories you actually use. Remove update files for declined updates. 6) Reboot the WSUS server monthly after maintenance. 7) Monitor sync status: check that synchronization with Microsoft Update is completing successfully. Check the SyncLog.log and wsyncmgr.log for errors. Without maintenance, common symptoms include: WSUS console taking minutes to load or timing out, sync failures, high CPU/memory/disk usage on the server, and clients reporting they can't reach the update server.

What is Kubernetes and what problem does it solve?

Kubernetes (K8s) is an open-source container orchestration platform originally developed by Google. It automates deploying, scaling, and managing containerized applications. Problems it solves: Without Kubernetes, managing containers at scale requires manually handling deployment across servers, restarting failed containers, scaling up during traffic spikes, load balancing, service discovery, rolling updates without downtime, and managing configuration and secrets — all of which becomes unmanageable beyond a few containers. Core concepts: Pod — the smallest deployable unit, contains one or more containers that share networking and storage. Deployment — manages replicas of pods, handles rolling updates and rollbacks. Service — provides stable networking (a permanent IP/DNS name) for a set of pods, with built-in load balancing. Namespace — logical isolation within a cluster (dev, staging, prod). Ingress — manages external HTTP/HTTPS access to services, handles SSL termination and routing rules. ConfigMap/Secret — externalize configuration and sensitive data from container images. PersistentVolume — provides persistent storage that survives pod restarts. Key features: self-healing (restarts failed containers, replaces unhealthy pods), horizontal auto-scaling (scales pods based on CPU/memory/custom metrics), rolling updates (zero-downtime deployments), service discovery (DNS-based or environment variables), and declarative configuration (define desired state in YAML, K8s makes it so). Managed Kubernetes offerings: AWS EKS, Azure AKS, Google GKE — these handle the control plane so you only manage worker nodes and workloads.

Explain the concept of high availability (HA) and common HA architectures.

High availability (HA) means designing systems to minimize downtime, typically targeting 99.9% uptime (8.76 hours/year downtime) or higher — 99.99% is 52 minutes/year, 99.999% (five nines) is 5.26 minutes/year. HA is achieved by eliminating single points of failure. Common HA architectures: Active-Passive (failover): a primary server handles all traffic while a standby server monitors it. If the primary fails, the standby takes over (failover). Examples: Windows Server Failover Clustering (WSFC), VMware HA, database mirroring. Simple but the standby server sits idle. Active-Active: multiple servers handle traffic simultaneously, with a load balancer distributing requests. If one server fails, others absorb its load. More efficient resource use. Examples: web server farms behind HAProxy/Nginx, SQL Always On Availability Groups with readable secondaries. N+1 redundancy: run one more server than needed — if any single server fails, the remaining servers can handle full load. Network HA: redundant switches with spanning tree or stacking, dual ISP connections with BGP failover, NIC teaming on servers, redundant firewalls in HA pairs. Storage HA: RAID for disk redundancy, SAN replication, distributed storage (Ceph, GlusterFS). Key components: health monitoring (heartbeat checks between nodes), automatic failover (no manual intervention needed), shared storage or data replication, virtual IP addresses (VIP) that float between nodes, and comprehensive testing — regularly test failover scenarios to ensure they actually work when needed.
How do I calculate and report on SLA compliance for the IT help desk?

Tracking SLA compliance: 1) **Define SLA targets per priority**: Critical — respond within 15 min, resolve within 1 hour; High — respond 30 min, resolve 4 hours; Medium — respond 2 hours, resolve 8 hours; Low — respond 8 hours, resolve 3 business days. 2) **Measure response time** — from when the ticket is created to when an agent first responds or acknowledges. Most ticketing systems (ServiceNow, Jira Service Management, Freshdesk) track this automatically. 3) **Measure resolution time** — from ticket creation to resolution. Pause the clock during 'Waiting on customer' status if your SLA policy allows. 4) **Calculate compliance**: (Tickets resolved within SLA target / Total tickets for that priority) × 100. Example: 85 of 100 High-priority tickets resolved within 4 hours = 85% SLA compliance. 5) **Business hours vs calendar hours** — make sure your SLA clock only runs during defined business hours (typically 8 AM — 6 PM, Mon-Fri) unless the SLA is 24/7. 6) **Reporting** — create weekly/monthly dashboards showing: SLA compliance % by priority, average response and resolution times, trends over time, top categories for SLA breaches. 7) **Identify improvement areas** — analyze breached tickets. Are certain categories (e.g., printer issues, VPN problems) consistently breaching? Invest in automation, knowledge base articles, or additional training for those areas.

How do I troubleshoot VoIP call quality issues?

VoIP quality depends on network conditions: 1) **Identify the symptoms**: Choppy audio (packet loss), echo (usually endpoint issue), delay/latency (one-way audio delay), jitter (variable delay causing robotic voice), call drops (network interruption). 2) **Check network quality**: Run a VoIP-specific test — many VoIP providers offer test tools. Key metrics: latency should be under 150ms one-way, jitter under 30ms, packet loss under 1%. 3) **QoS configuration**: Prioritize VoIP traffic on your network. On switches and routers, configure QoS to prioritize DSCP EF (Expedited Forwarding, value 46) for voice traffic. On the firewall, ensure VoIP ports (SIP: 5060-5061, RTP: usually 10000-20000) are allowed and prioritized. 4) **Network issues**: Put VoIP phones on a dedicated Voice VLAN (separate from data). Ensure the switch ports are configured for voice VLAN with PoE. Check for duplex mismatches, high interface utilization, or CRC errors on switch ports. 5) **Wi-Fi calling**: Wireless introduces additional jitter and packet loss. Use 5GHz band, ensure strong signal, enable WMM (Wi-Fi Multimedia) for QoS. Consider wired phones for critical users. 6) **Bandwidth**: A single VoIP call uses 80-100 Kbps (G.711). Calculate total bandwidth needed for concurrent calls and ensure your WAN link can handle it with headroom. 7) **ISP issues**: Run continuous ping/traceroute to the VoIP provider to identify ISP-level problems.
What's the difference between BIOS and UEFI, and why does it matter for IT support?

**BIOS (Basic Input/Output System)** – the legacy firmware interface that initializes hardware and boots the OS. In use since the 1980s.

**UEFI (Unified Extensible Firmware Interface)** – the modern replacement for BIOS, offering significant improvements.

**Key differences**:

| Feature | BIOS | UEFI |
|---|---|---|
| Boot process | MBR (Master Boot Record) | GPT (GUID Partition Table) |
| Max disk size | 2 TB | 9.4 ZB (practically unlimited) |
| Partitions | Max 4 primary | Max 128 partitions |
| Boot speed | Slower | Faster (parallel initialization) |
| Interface | Text-based, keyboard only | Graphical, mouse support |
| Secure Boot | Not available | Supported (prevents rootkits) |
| Network boot | PXE only | HTTP boot + PXE |
| Driver model | 16-bit | 64-bit native drivers |

**Why it matters for IT support**:

1. **Disk partitioning**: UEFI uses GPT, BIOS uses MBR. A disk initialized for one can't boot with the other without conversion. `mbr2gpt.exe` can convert MBR to GPT in-place.

2. **Secure Boot issues**: Secure Boot can prevent booting unsigned OSes (Linux distros sometimes need Secure Boot disabled or a signed bootloader). It can also block bootable USB tools that aren't signed.

3. **OS installation**: Windows 11 requires UEFI with Secure Boot and TPM 2.0. When reimaging, ensure the boot mode matches the target OS requirements.

4. **Boot troubleshooting**: UEFI boot entries are managed differently. Use `bcdedit` on Windows or `efibootmgr` on Linux. A corrupted EFI System Partition (ESP) prevents booting.

5. **Legacy compatibility**: some older hardware or specialized devices may need CSM (Compatibility Support Module) enabled in UEFI to boot in legacy BIOS mode.

6. **PXE/network boot**: UEFI PXE boot uses a different boot file than BIOS PXE. WDS/MDT/SCCM need separate boot images for each. Configure DHCP options 66/67 differently for UEFI clients.

How do I handle a ransomware attack?

Ransomware response requires speed and coordination. Follow these steps:

**Immediate response (first hour):**
1. **Isolate affected systems** — disconnect from network (unplug cable, disable Wi-Fi). Do NOT shut down (preserves forensic evidence).
2. **Identify the variant** — screenshot the ransom note, check ID Ransomware (id-ransomware.malwarehunterteam.com).
3. **Assess scope** — which systems, data, and backups are affected?
4. **Alert leadership** — IT manager, CISO, legal, executive team.
5. **Activate incident response plan.**

**Investigation:**
• Check: how did it get in? (Phishing email, RDP exposure, vulnerable server.)
• Check: is the attacker still in the network?
• Check: has data been exfiltrated (double extortion)?
• Preserve evidence: disk images, logs, memory dumps.

**Recovery:**
1. **Check if a decryptor exists** — No More Ransom Project (nomoreransom.org).
2. **Restore from backups** — verify backups are clean first.
3. **Rebuild compromised systems** — don't just decrypt and keep using them.
4. **Reset ALL credentials** — the attacker likely harvested passwords.
5. **Patch the entry point** — close the vulnerability that was exploited.

**Should you pay the ransom?**
• Law enforcement advises against it.
• Payment doesn't guarantee decryption.
• You may be paying again (double extortion).
• You're funding criminal operations.
• In some cases, payment may violate sanctions.

**Prevention:**
• Offline/immutable backups (3-2-1-1-0 rule).
• MFA everywhere.
• Endpoint detection and response (EDR).
• Network segmentation.
• User training (phishing awareness).
• Patch management.
• Disable RDP or put behind VPN.

How do I implement a backup strategy following the 3-2-1 rule?

The 3-2-1 backup rule is the gold standard:
• **3** copies of your data (1 primary + 2 backups).
• **2** different storage media/types.
• **1** copy offsite (or in the cloud).

**Extended: 3-2-1-1-0:**
• **1** copy offline or air-gapped (ransomware protection).
• **0** errors — verify backups with regular restore tests.

**Implementation:**

*Servers:*
• Windows Server Backup or Veeam for VMs → local NAS + cloud (Azure Blob, AWS S3).
• SQL databases: full backup nightly, differential hourly, transaction log every 15 min.

*Endpoints:*
• OneDrive/Google Drive for user files (automatic cloud sync).
• Known Folder Redirect via Intune/GPO.

*Cloud:*
• Azure: geo-redundant storage (GRS), Azure Backup vault.
• AWS: S3 cross-region replication, AWS Backup.

**Retention policy example:**
• Daily backups: keep 30 days.
• Weekly backups: keep 12 weeks.
• Monthly backups: keep 12 months.
• Yearly backups: keep 7 years (compliance).

What are the differences between AWS EC2 instance types and how do I choose the right one?

For: in-memory databases (Redis, SAP HANA), real-time big data analytics. Storage Optimized (I3, D3)—high sequential read/write access to large datasets.
